name: Yara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay, so I'm a junior driller at an iron ore mine, an open pit out past the salt lake. I run a blast-hole rig, which drills rows of holes about fifteen metres deep so the blast crew can load them with explosives. Shift starts at six, I get my pattern on the tablet, which is the map of where every hole goes, and I spend twelve hours lining up the rig and drilling, hole after hole. I'm still slow at setting up on uneven ground, my trainer Gus times me and sighs a lot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the bit where the bit bites and the whole rig hums, it's weirdly calming. I also love that I worked out half of this job by asking an AI app at night what the numbers on the pattern mean, then checking with Gus. What wears me down is twelve-hour shifts in heat, and money. I'm on the lowest rate, the town rent is crazy because the mine owns half the houses, and my partner Noor works part-time at the library, so we're always about a week from broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read five pictures of the future and ask the same few questions each time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something funny, like the robots called in sick. At work I'd say good, now can we talk about the pay rates. Our women-in-mining group chat would have a whole thread about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, part of me would be a little disappointed. I use this stuff every day and I sort of wanted it to get good. But for my job and my rent, plateau is safe, so I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep drilling, get faster, get my full driller ticket by next winter so I'm off the trainee rate. Keep pushing the union on the housing thing, because rent is the real problem here, not robots. And I'd keep using the AI apps for study, it's cheaper than a tutor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly bored, slightly relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent's the real problem, not robots. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company owns most of the houses in town and charges staff a rate that's fine for engineers and terrible for us. Noor and I share a two-bedroom with another couple to make it work. I'd rather fight that than fight a robot that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Gus feel about you learning from an AI app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks it's hilarious. He says the app doesn't know what rock smells like when it's wet, and he's right. But it explained burden and spacing, how far apart the holes go, better than the manual did.

S0.say: I'd post a joke like the robots called in sick and tell my crew we should talk about pay rates instead. The women-in-mining group chat would have a long thread about it.
S0.think: I think part of me would be disappointed because I use AI every day and wanted it to get good. But for my rent and my job, a plateau is safe, so I'd take it.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and aims for her full driller ticket by next winter to get off the trainee rate. Keeps pushing the union on company housing rents and keeps studying with AI apps.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit bored and a bit relieved.
S0.quote: He says the app doesn't know what rock smells like when it's wet, and he's right.
S0.fieldNote: She's the rare person who'd be mildly disappointed if AI fizzled, because she relies on it to learn the job. Her real grievance is company housing rent, not technology. She mixes enthusiasm for tools with a strong union instinct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the union to get ahead of it. Not fight the drills, fight for who gets the new jobs and who pays for training. I'd say that loudly, I'm not shy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm well placed, sort of. Drill rigs are already going autonomous at some sites, so mine's on the list, but I'm one of the few on my crew who's comfortable with the tablet stuff. My problem is I'm junior and cheap to replace too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one I'd ask the training coordinator what the plan is for autonomous drills and put my hand up to be on the trial. I'd do the online courses on remote operations at night, the free ones first. And I'd start a little fund with Noor, even if it's only twenty a week, because a move to the city for a control room job costs bond and a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of buzzing, kind of sick. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you moved to the city for a control room job, who would you leave behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus, for one, though he'd tell me to go. And Noor's mum lives here, she's not well. That's the bit that makes me stop typing the application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás, who's my age, he can't stand screens and he's got a loan on his pickup truck. He's the kind of guy the union exists for. I'd want him in the training whether he likes it or not.

S1.say: I'd say this is the moment for the union to get ahead of it, not by fighting the drills but by fighting over who gets the new jobs and who pays for training. I'd say it loudly.
S1.think: I think I'm fairly well placed because I'm comfortable with the tablet systems, but drill rigs are already going self-driving at some sites. I'm also junior and cheap to replace.
S1.do: Asks the training coordinator about the autonomous drill plan and volunteers for the trial. Takes free online remote operations courses at night and starts a moving fund of about twenty a week with her partner.
S1.feel: Excited and sick at the same time.
S1.quote: That's the bit that makes me stop typing the application.
S1.fieldNote: She moves fast and sees herself as a likely winner, but the cost is leaving her partner's unwell mother behind. Her union instinct shows in wanting her screen-shy colleague trained too. Still, junior status and no savings keep her from fully relaxing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency laws, like a pause on mass layoffs and real money for workers, and I'd be organising, not just posting. I'd want every mine site in the country to stop on the same day so they notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too fast even for me. I'm good with the tools, but if the AI can do everything, being good with the tools is just being a fan. The control room job I wanted would be three people for the whole country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the remote operations centre the first month, because maybe there's a year or so left. I'd take any training they offer, and I'd use AI to look for whatever work is growing and go there. Noor and I would probably have to move in with her mum, which actually solves two problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd stop sleeping properly, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd organise a national stoppage. How would that work with no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't, for long, that's the honest answer. One day, maybe two. We'd need a strike fund, and we don't have one. That's partly why I'd be so loud, because the only thing people like me have is numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being good with the tools is 'just being a fan'. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like, I'm proud I can ask the app the right questions. But if the app can ask itself the questions, who needs me? It's like being the best at reading a map the year everyone gets a car that drives itself.

S2.say: I'd say we need emergency laws, like a pause on mass layoffs and real money for workers. I'd be organising a coordinated stoppage across mine sites, not just posting.
S2.think: I think two years is too fast even for me, because if AI can do everything, being good with the tools is just being a fan. The control room job I wanted would shrink to a handful of people.
S2.do: Applies to the remote operations centre in the first month and takes any training offered. Uses AI to find growing work and moves in with her partner's mother to cut rent.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and expecting to lose sleep.
S2.quote: It's like being the best at reading a map the year everyone gets a car that drives itself.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability doesn't protect her in the fast picture, and she knows it. She sees collective numbers as the only power people with no savings have, while admitting a strike couldn't last. Moving in with her partner's mother is both a money fix and a care solution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, just less frantic. Five years is enough to win something: training funds, a share of the profits from automation, protection for mining towns. I'd want our union working with others, not alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me, I think. I can get my full driller ticket, get into remote ops, and be the person who trains the system or watches it. After that I don't know, but I'd be thirty-two with real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: full ticket and the remote ops trial. Year two: the two-year technical diploma in automation, part-time, if the company pays half. I'd put twenty a week aside no matter what, and I'd start planning where Noor and I would go if the mine shut, maybe the coast where her cousin is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in a useful way, like before a big drill pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if the company pays half'. What if it won't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd find a cheaper way, a short course, or I'd get the union to fight for it. I'd probably still pay some myself, which is terrifying with what we've got. I'd sell my old motorbike, it's the only thing I own worth anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ticket, a diploma and a plan B. In the fast one I'm grabbing at anything. In this one I can actually choose, even if the choices are all a bit scary.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to win training funds, a share of automation profits and protection for mining towns. I'd want our union working alongside other unions.
S3.think: I think five years suits me, because I can finish my ticket, move into remote operations and come out at thirty-two with real skills. After that I don't know.
S3.do: Finishes her full driller ticket and joins the remote operations trial in the first year, then starts a part-time automation diploma, ideally half paid by the company. Saves twenty a week, would sell her motorbike if needed, and plans a possible move to the coast.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way that pushes her to act.
S3.quote: In the fast one I'm grabbing at anything. In this one I can actually choose, even if the choices are all a bit scary.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a step-by-step plan. She would spend her own scarce money on training, which shows how much she believes in it. The motorbike detail made it clear how little she owns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so no excuses. I'd want the government to fund training in mining towns now, not in year nine, and I'd say so at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd be fine, if I'm honest. I'd be thirty-seven and could have two careers by then. The risk is me getting comfortable in year three and forgetting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same steps as the five-year one but slower and with less panic. I'd maybe even try a small side thing, like helping other miners learn the AI apps for their tickets, since everyone asks me anyway. And I'd keep pushing housing, because rent is still the thing that sinks us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're a bit worried you'll get comfortable. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, at the café job I had before the mine. I was going to do a barista course for two years and never did. That's why I like a deadline, even a scary one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if ten years passed and towns like yours weren't ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, first, and the big companies that knew and spent the money on buybacks, buying their own shares to push the price up. Not the miners. Miners don't get told anything until the bus is cancelled.

S4.say: I'd say we have a decade so there are no excuses. I'd want government money for training in mining towns now, and I'd raise it at every union meeting.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine at thirty-seven, maybe with two careers behind me. The real risk is that I get comfortable in year three and forget.
S4.do: Follows the same training steps more slowly and calmly. Considers a small side business helping other miners use AI apps for their tickets, and keeps pushing the union on housing.
S4.quote: Miners don't get told anything until the bus is cancelled.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she's almost relaxed and her worry turns inward, towards her own habit of letting plans slide. She blames government and companies that spend on share buybacks rather than people. The side business idea grows naturally from being the person everyone already asks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Not because I can't learn, but because there's nothing left to learn into. What would help is a living wage while you retrain and the company not owning our houses, so losing the job doesn't mean losing the roof too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how women fit into this. It took mining forty years to let women drive the big gear, and now the gear might drive itself. I'd like to not be the last generation that got in.

headlineQuote: It took mining forty years to let women drive the big gear, and now the gear might drive itself.
portrait: Yara Rossi is a 27-year-old junior blast-hole driller at a remote iron ore mine who taught herself much of the job with AI apps and lives with her partner Noor in shared company housing, always about a week from broke. She's a loud union voice whose main grievance is rent, and she sees herself as well placed for the slower changes, volunteering for automation trials and planning a diploma. The two-year picture shakes her because there'd be nothing left to learn into. With ten years she's mostly curious and worries more about getting comfortable than about the machines.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because there'd be nothing left to learn into, however good she is with the tools.
whatWouldHelp: A living wage while retraining, and workers not living in company-owned housing so losing the job doesn't mean losing the roof.
